newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban dissidents face "enemy propaganda" charge.
newsitem.headline: Cuban dissidents face "enemy propaganda" charge.

text.p: Four Cuban dissidents arrested more than a week ago by Cuban police will be charged with "enemy propaganda", a fellow dissident and the lawyer of one of them said on Thursday.

The four -- Vladimiro Roca, Martha Beatriz Roque, Felix Bonne and Rene Gomez Manzano -- were detained July 16 and are being held at Villa Marista, the Havana headquarters of Cuba's state security police.
Tania Quintero, a dissident journalist and colleague of the four, told foreign correspondents in Havana that Roca's lawyer, Amelia Rodriguez, visited her client at Villa Marista on Thursday.

She was told by state security officers in charge of the case that all four would be charged with "enemy propaganda", a crime specified in Cuba's Penal Code under the chapter of "Crimes against the internal security of the state".
The Cuban government has not said when the detained dissidents might go on trial.
The crime of "enemy propaganda" carries a possible jail term of between one and eight years and more in extreme cases.
It is a charge frequently used by Cuba's communist authorities to prosecute internal opponents of one-party rule.
Rodriguez called one foreign news agency office in Havana on Thursday to inform reporters of the development in the case of the four detained dissidents.
Cuban authorities have not publicly announced formal charges against the four, who are members of a group calling itself the "Internal Dissidence Working Group".

But Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Marianela Ferriol confirmed on Thursday that the ministry had sent a diplomatic note to the Canadian and Netherlands embassies explaining the accusations that led to the arrest of the four.
The note said they were being held because they had threatened foreign investors, lied about the economy and tried to disrupt upcoming one-party elections.

The Cuban note responded to representations made last Friday by diplomats from Canada and the Netherlands, acting on behalf of the European Union, in which the foreign diplomats expressed their governments' concern about the arrests.
The July 22 Cuban diplomatic note said the four detained had been engaged in "intense activity aimed at subverting the legal and constitutional order of the Republic of Cuba".
The note also said: "The Cuban authorities have sufficient proof of the involvement of these citizens with leaders of terrorist groups based in the territory of the United States."
But it did not specifically link the detained dissidents to the explosion of two small bombs in two central Havana hotels on July 12. Three people were slightly injured in the blasts.

Cuban authorities made clear that they believed right- wing anti-communist Cuban exiles in Miami were behind the recent bomb blasts, which Cuban officials said appeared to be aimed at damaging the island's growing tourist industry.
The U.S. government has asked Cuba to provide evidence to support an initial accusation that the people and materials involved in the bombings came from the United States.
